Pool and lanai turf for Ocoee homes

Pool and lanai turf in Ocoee runs the $8–$18 per square foot residential range as of September 2026, typically $10–$16. Subdivisions built from the 1990s forward favor a screened cage that needs a drainage underlay at the deck, while older, uncaged pools near Starke Lake take more direct sun.

Reviewed by Luis Austin, owner · Last reviewed September 21, 2026

Turf inside a screened cage in a newer Ocoee subdivision

Subdivisions built from the 1990s forward, Wesmere and the growth-era neighborhoods off Maguire and Clarke Road included, favor a screened pool cage over an open deck, which leaves a ring of shaded turf between the cage frame and the pool coping that sod rarely holds up in. Turf in that enclosure needs a drainage underlay wherever it meets the concrete deck, since the screen blocks some rain while wind-driven storms still reach the area a few times a season.

Glue-down edges against the slab hold up better than a nailed perimeter would inside any screen enclosure, regardless of which Ocoee neighborhood the pool sits in.

Why the ground near the pump pad stays wetter than the rest of the yard

The equipment pad next to a pool, where the pump and filter sit, sheds backwash and drips more consistently than any other spot on a Ocoee lot, and turf bordering that pad needs the same washed rock depth and undisturbed native sand as anywhere else to keep that extra moisture moving down instead of sitting at the surface. Compacting the soil under that section too hard, which is easy to do when equipment traffic has already packed it down over the years, works against the percolation the state's turf standard requires. A border here often needs a fresh pass of loosening before rock goes down.

Older, uncaged pools near Starke Lake

Closer to downtown, pools built before Ocoee's growth era often went in without a screen enclosure, since cages weren't standard practice on the city's older lake-town lots. Turf around an uncovered pool takes full sun in a way a shaded, caged one never does, pushing the surface toward the upper end of the 120 to 150 degree range and making a lighter-colored or cooling infill worth the added cost right along the deck.

This article covers product and infill choices that hold up well against pool coping specifically. Older, uncaged pools turn up just as often in Winter Garden and Gotha.

Brushing infill up to a hard glued edge instead of a soft one

Infill along a nailed perimeter on soil settles and shifts slightly as the ground below moves with moisture, but infill against a glued edge on a Ocoee pool deck sits against a perimeter that never moves at all, since it is bonded straight to concrete or set into a coping line. That fixed edge means infill brushed at the standard one to two pounds per square foot holds its finished line more predictably along a lanai floor than along a border with a soft, nailed perimeter, where a slightly heavier hand near the edge helps offset the natural settling a soil-backed perimeter still does over its first season.

Say you have a 520 sq ft turf strip inside a screened cage in a 2008 Ocoee home

Say you have a 520 sq ft strip of turf planned inside the screened pool cage of a 2008 home off Maguire Road, running along two sides of the deck where sod never fully took hold in the shade cast by the enclosure's frame. At the $10–$16 per sq ft range pool-area turf typically lands in, that project prices between $5,200 and $8,320, usually toward the upper half because glue-down edges over concrete take more labor than a nailed perimeter in open ground.

A drainage underlay goes down first wherever the turf meets the slab, since the screen keeps most rain off but a wind-driven storm still reaches that strip a few times a year. Once that layer is in, the rest of the build looks like any other turf job, just anchored to concrete rather than soil at the edges.

Building a border and a glued floor as one sequenced job

When a Ocoee property gets both an open deck border and a glued lanai floor at the same visit, the rock base for the border goes in and compacts first, before the slab gets pressure washed for the glue-down section, so dust and loose fines from the soil work do not land on a clean, prepped slab. Compacting the border early also gives that section time to settle while the crew finishes prepping and gluing the floor, rather than rushing both areas to be ready on the same afternoon. The two areas finish on the same day even though they are built in a different order.

Keeping a shaded pool corner outside an oak's root zone

A mature oak shading part of a Ocoee pool deck sounds like the ideal spot for turf that stays cooler through the afternoon, but the drip-line rule applies here exactly as it does anywhere else on the lot: no turf inside the canopy's root zone without a certified arborist's letter confirming the install will not harm the tree. Digging even a shallow lanai-floor edge or a border's rock base near exposed surface roots close to the trunk can do real damage before anyone notices. Getting that letter before committing to a shaded layout is the only way to use the space legally.

Why Ocoee's watering-day rules skip a pool deck

Ocoee's odd-and-even irrigation schedule governs sprinkler zones, and a pool deck strip usually was never on one of those zones to begin with (the city’s watering schedule). Where a head did reach that area, capping it is required under the state's turf standard regardless of the day printed on a water bill, and the pool itself becomes the closest thing to a scheduled rinse the turf gets, since a quick hose-off after a swim covers the same job.

That's one less watering zone to plan around than a full front-yard conversion, where grass on either side of the driveway often still needs its own schedule.

Keeping the deck drain clear inside a screen enclosure

A screen mesh keeps most large debris out of a Ocoee lanai, but pollen, dust, and small leaves still settle on the turf and can work toward the deck drain over time, especially during the June-to-September rainy season when storms are frequent enough that the drain rarely gets a rest. A quick sweep or rinse toward the drain on a regular schedule keeps the whole underlay system doing what it was built for, since even a permeable backing cannot help much once the drain it feeds is the part that is actually clogged.

Questions people ask

Does turf inside an Ocoee pool cage need a different base than an open yard?

Yes, where it meets the concrete deck. A drainage underlay handles water the screen doesn't fully block, and the perimeter gets glued to the slab instead of nailed the way an open-ground edge would be.

Is pool-area turf hotter in an older, uncovered Ocoee pool than a caged one?

Generally yes, since a screen enclosure blocks some direct sun an open deck gets all day. A lighter-colored or cooling infill, along with hosing the area down on hot afternoons, both help close that gap.

Do I need a permit for turf around a pool in Ocoee?

Nothing published singles out pool-area turf from any other synthetic turf project in the city. Call the Building Division at 407-905-3104 if the pool cage itself is part of the scope, since a structural change can trigger its own review.
